meta.title: Three of Our Graduates
meta.skill_frame: Argument and evidence: a list of successes offered as a rate.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured FK 5.73, 5.85 and 6.37 on the three parts (102, 102 and 100 words), 5.98 together. The ad lists three winners from a class of thirty-one, so the reader has to track who is missing from the list before reading it as a rate.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.attribution: Original text drafted for argument_evidence 4.3, band 4.3, sequence 3. No external work.
source.text_status: Drafted for the band, accepted on spot check.
source.survey: A course advertisement that names its three most successful graduates and leaves out the size of the class.
source.avoided: No school name, town, or newspaper name.

session.difficulty_basis: Three shop owners are named from a class of thirty-one, and the ad never says what happened to the other twenty-eight.

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: A welding course runs an advertisement in the local paper. The ad says the course leads to steady work, and it names its proof in the second line. Three graduates now run their own repair shops, the ad says, and it gives the town and the year each one finished. All three stories are true, and the shops are open six days a week. Three shop owners from one course sounds like a strong result for a class that meets twice a week in a rented room. The ad repeats the number three in its headline and again in the last line.
passage.part_2: The ad does not say how many people started the course. The program's own enrollment sheet, printed in the same paper a year earlier, listed thirty-one students for that class. The sheet does not say how many finished, or how many of those found work in a shop. A list of the ones who did well is easy to write, and it says nothing about the rest, who paid the same fee. The three owners may be the best of thirty-one, or the best of three. The ad leaves the reader to guess, and the guess runs toward the headline.
passage.part_3: A list of successes answers a different question from the one the ad asks. The ad claims the course leads to steady work, and the list shows that steady work is possible after the course. Possible and usual are not the same thing, and an ad may sell the first while claiming the second. The missing number is the one that would make the claim testable: how many started, and what happened to each of them. The ad has that enrollment sheet, or knows where to find it. Until the number appears, three shops are three stories, not a rate.
